What is the difference between drawback and RoDTEP?

Duty drawback refunds customs duty and central excise paid on inputs used to make the export product. RoDTEP refunds other taxes and levies that are not refunded anywhere else, such as VAT on fuel, mandi tax and electricity duty. They cover different taxes, so you can claim both on the same shipment.

Can AA, EOU and SEZ exporters get RoDTEP?

Yes. Since {0}, exports by Advance Authorisation holders, EOUs and SEZ units get RoDTEP at the Appendix {1}RE rates, which are lower than the Appendix {2}R rates for regular exporters. They cannot claim All Industry Rate drawback.
Why do I have to pick a drawback line?

The drawback schedule follows the Customs Tariff only at the {0}-digit heading. Below that it has its own sub-items, for example by fibre for garments. Pick the line that describes your goods; we pre-select our best match.
What is the cap per unit?
Many drawback, RoDTEP and RoSCTL lines have a maximum amount per kilogram, piece or other unit. You get the lower of the percentage of FOB and the cap multiplied by your quantity.
How do I actually receive these benefits?

Your customs broker claims them on the shipping bill. Drawback is paid into your bank account after the export is completed. RoDTEP and RoSCTL are issued as transferable e-scrips on ICEGATE, which you can use to pay import duty or sell to other importers.

Type what you are shipping, like “cotton t-shirts” or “solar panels”, and see the likely {0}-digit HSN codes from the Indian Customs Tariff, with the headline duty and the import and export policy for each.
From product to HSN code, in three steps.
Type what it is in everyday words, what it is made of and what it does. Or type the first digits of a code you already have.
Results are grouped by chapter. Pick the chapter that fits, then read the full description path to find the line that matches your goods.
Open the duty or export benefit for that code in one click, then send it to our desk to confirm before you file.
Four questions that decide the code
Material decides the chapter for most goods: a cotton shirt and a polyester shirt have different codes. Include the main material in your search.
Machines and electronics are classified by their function. Search for what it does (“pump”, “charger”, “router”) rather than a brand or model name.
Parts often have their own lines, usually ending in “parts”. If you ship parts, add the word “parts” to your search.
Clothing is split between Chapter {0} (knitted) and Chapter {1} (woven). A T-shirt is usually knitted; a formal shirt is usually woven.

HSN (Harmonized System of Nomenclature) is the international system for classifying goods. The first {0} digits are the same worldwide; India adds {1} more to make the {2}-digit ITC(HS) or Customs Tariff code used on bills of entry, shipping bills and GST invoices.
Is the HSN code the same for import, export and GST?
The {0}-digit code is the same in the Customs Tariff and ITC(HS) for import and export. GST invoices usually show {1}, {2} or {3} digits depending on turnover, but they follow the same structure.
Why do I get several possible codes?

Many products can sound alike in words but fall in different chapters depending on material, function or whether they are parts. The finder shows every line that matches your words; the right one is the line whose full description, read with the chapter notes, fits your goods.
Can I rely on the code the finder suggests?

No. It is a starting point for guidance only. The code you declare is your responsibility, and a wrong code can cost you duty, penalties or export benefits. Ask a licensed customs broker to confirm, or apply for an advance ruling if the case is unclear.
What does Restricted or Prohibited mean?

This is the ITC(HS) import or export policy for the code. Free means no licence is needed under that policy. Restricted needs a DGFT authorisation or must meet conditions. Prohibited cannot be imported or exported. State trading means only notified state agencies may trade it.

How is Indian import duty calculated?

Basic customs duty (BCD) is charged on the assessable value, which is the CIF value converted at the CBIC customs exchange rate. If freight or insurance is not known, customs practice is to add {2}% of the FOB value for freight and {3}% for insurance. Social welfare surcharge (SWS) is normally {4}% of the BCD. IGST is then charged on the assessable value plus BCD and SWS. Some goods also attract agriculture cess (AIDC), compensation cess, anti-dumping or safeguard duty.

{0}. Information that stays on your device

The calculations in our tools run inside the app or your browser. This includes the cargo lists, dimensions and weights you type into the container load planner, the PDFs and loading videos it creates, CBM and duty calculations, and the invoices, packing lists, bills of lading or airway bills you open in the document checker. These are not uploaded to us.
To work well, the app keeps a few small items on your device:
your recent tracking searches, so you can repeat them quickly;
the results you choose to save, your
list (numbers, labels, ETAs and notes), and the details you type into the invoice and packing list maker and its checklist, so you do not have to enter them again;
small notes that you have already seen a notice, cleared when you close the app;
offline copies of our pages and tools, so they work without signal.
You can remove all of these by clearing the app’s storage in Android settings (Settings › Apps › CargoKit › Storage), or by clearing site data in your browser.
{0}. Information sent when you use live tools

When the app or site loads a page, your device connects to our hosting provider, Cloudflare. As with any website, this connection includes your IP address, browser type, the page requested and the time. Cloudflare processes this to deliver and protect the site, under its own privacy policy.

When you search a vessel name, container number or airway bill, that search text is sent to our server so it can look up public vessel information. We do not attach your name or contact details to it and we do not keep a record of who searched. Links to carriers’ and airlines’ own tracking pages open their websites, which have their own privacy policies.

The duty calculator and export benefit finder fetch current exchange rates from our server and from public rate services (frankfurter.dev and open.er-api.com). The Trade Desk fetches public news and government notices. These requests contain no personal information beyond the normal connection details above.

If you turn on alerts in My shipments, you give us your email address or WhatsApp number, and we confirm it with a one-time code. Which Latin American countries have a trade agreement with India?

Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay through the India–Mercosur PTA, and Chile through the India–Chile PTA. A deal with Peru and a wider agreement with Chile are being negotiated, and talks to expand the Mercosur PTA started in September {0}. All other countries apply normal (MFN) duties to Indian goods.
How long does sea freight from India to South America take?

Roughly {0}–{1} days to the east coast (Santos, Buenos Aires, Montevideo), {2}–{3} days to the west coast (Callao, San Antonio, Guayaquil), and {4}–{5} days to Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean, depending on transhipment.
What do Indian exporters sell most to Latin America?

Vehicles and motorcycles, chemicals and agrochemicals, machinery, pharmaceuticals, textiles and yarn, and petroleum products. India buys gold, crude oil, soybean and sunflower oil, copper concentrate and sugar.
Did Mexico raise tariffs on Indian goods?

Yes. From January {0} Mexico raised tariffs on about {1} tariff lines from countries without a trade agreement with it, including India, to rates of up to {2}%. Vehicles, auto parts, steel, textiles and machinery are the most affected.
Can YAM handle shipments door to door in Latin America?
Yes. YAM handles export clearance and freight from India, and our partner agents handle destination clearance and delivery across Latin America. We do the same in reverse for imports into India.
